ta-l1d19q4-d1e3498.summary: A divisio textus for Lombard's second proof of the persons' equal magnitude, by removing what could cause inequality, and his third, from truth. The persons do not share the essence as parts in an integral whole: an integral whole requires parts diverse in essence, and as the Father is not composed of his many attributes, the divine nature is not composed of persons. Nor do they share it as species or individuals in a universal whole: a genus is predicated in the plural of several species ('a man and a donkey are animals'), but we do not say the three persons are three essences, and what is numerically one has no species or individuals under it. Nor do they share it as matter: several rings have more gold than one, but three persons do not have more essence than one. Nor as a formal property, like humans of the same complexion, where two are more than one. Lombard reconciles Damascene's talk of essence as species and persons as particulars, and of hypostases differing in number, not nature, by a likeness and by relational distinction. Third, where truth and magnitude are the same, there is no greater magnitude where there is no greater truth, and it is no more true that three persons are than that one is, so three are not greater than one. Hence God is called triune but not triple. Two articles are announced: whether there is an integral whole in God, and whether there is a universal whole.
claims: The persons do not share the essence as parts of a whole, as species of a genus, as things made of one matter, or as bearers of a common property.
Three persons are not greater than one, so God is triune, not triple.

ta-l1d19q4-d1e3553.summary: First argument for an integral whole in God. Wherever there is quantity there is the character of an integral whole, since all quantity is divisible into parts, and in God there is quantity of power.
claims: All quantity is divisible into parts.

ta-l1d19q4-d1e3556.summary: Second argument. As continuous quantity is integrated from its parts, so is number, and in God there is a number of persons, three, of which one and two are parts.
claims: Number is integrated from its parts.

ta-l1d19q4-d1e3559.summary: Third argument. Whatever is something of another and is not that other is its integral part. The Father is something of the Trinity and is not the Trinity, so he is an integral part of it.
claims: The Father is something of the Trinity without being the Trinity.

ta-l1d19q4-d1e3563.summary: Fourth argument. Things of a nature are never constituted from the nature alone, especially where there are several in one nature, and in the one divine nature there are several things of the nature, the persons. So something else must be added to the divine nature to constitute a person, and something will be integrated from several.
claims: Supposits are not constituted by nature alone.

ta-l1d19q4-d1e3566.summary: Sed contra. Every integral whole is composed of parts, and in God there is no composition but supreme simplicity (Dist. 8).
claims: God is supremely simple.

ta-l1d19q4-d1e3569.summary: Thomas's determination. The concept of an integral whole consists in composition, and the concept of an integral part carries imperfection, both of which conflict with divine simplicity and perfection, so there can be no integral whole and part in God.
claims: There is no integral whole or part in God, since these imply composition and imperfection.

ta-l1d19q4-d1e3572.summary: Reply to the first argument. Quantity of power is not measured by internal division of the power but by its division relative to external things, by number of objects, intensity of act, or modes of acting. So quantity of power has no character of integral whole and part, since integral parts are within their whole.
claims: Quantity of power is divided externally, so it has no integral parts.

ta-l1d19q4-d1e3575.summary: Reply to the second argument. In God unity or duality is part of the ternary only conceptually, because number and unity are found differently in divine and created things. The one is what is undivided in itself and divided from others. Each created thing is distinguished from others by its essence, so its essence, as undivided in itself and distinguishing from others, is its unity, and several unities constituting a number of created persons are several essences gathered by numbering, with nothing numerically the same in one and another. So number in creatures involves distinction and a kind of aggregation of things distinct in essence, and from this it has the character of an integral whole. Personal unity is the relative property distinguishing one person from another, not the person's essence, so the three persons do not differ in essence, since numerically one essence is in all three. So there is no aggregation, only distinction, and number has no character of an integral whole, except perhaps as the concepts of the personal properties are gathered in the intellect, which integrates nothing real but only a concept.
claims: Number in creatures aggregates essences; in God it signifies only distinction by relations without aggregation.
The divine ternary is not an integral whole except conceptually.

ta-l1d19q4-d1e3578.summary: Reply to the third argument. 'The Father is something (aliquid) of the Trinity' is false if understood partitively, since it would signify that he has part of the Trinity's essence, 'aliquid', being neuter, signifying essence. But 'he is someone (aliquis) of the Trinity' is true, and from it one can conclude only that he is a part conceptually, since he is not as many persons as the Trinity: the Trinity is three persons, and the Father is not.
claims: The Father is 'aliquis' but not 'aliquid' of the Trinity.

ta-l1d19q4-d1e3582.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. Nothing is added to the divine nature to constitute a thing of the nature, since in God 'that by which he is' and 'that which (or who) he is' are the same. Distinction comes not from the concept of nature but from the relative property, which compared to the essence differs only conceptually and compared to its opposed correlative makes a real distinction of person (Dist. 9).
claims: Nothing is added to the divine nature to constitute a person; the relative property is conceptually identical with the essence and really distinct from its correlative.

ta-l1d19q4-d1e3594.summary: First argument for a universal whole in God. Whatever is predicated of something substantially and not conversely is predicated of it as a universal whole of a subjective part, and the divine essence or God is so predicated of the Father: the Father is the divine essence, but not whatever is the divine essence is the Father.
claims: Non-convertible substantial predication is that of universal of particular.

ta-l1d19q4-d1e3597.summary: Second argument. Universal and particular differ as common and proper, and in God there is common (the essence) and proper (relation).
claims: Common and proper exist in God.

ta-l1d19q4-d1e3600.summary: Third argument. Hilary says the Son of God exercised the power of his genus in the garb of the assumed humanity, and 'genus' names his nature, so the essence seems a genus and universal relative to the persons.
claims: Hilary speaks of the Son's 'genus'.

ta-l1d19q4-d1e3607.summary: Fourth argument. Science is a species of cognition, and both are said of God, who cognizes and knows.
claims: Both genus and species are predicated of God.

ta-l1d19q4-d1e3610.summary: Sed contra. Wherever there is universal and particular, the particulars are in potency in their universals, like differences in a genus, and in God nothing is in potency.
claims: Particulars are potentially in universals.

ta-l1d19q4-d1e3613.summary: Second sed contra. Every superior is an integral part constituting the definition of the inferior: genus is like matter, difference like form, species like the composite (Porphyry). In God there is no integral whole and part, so no universal whole either.
claims: Genus and difference are like matter and form.

ta-l1d19q4-d1e3616.summary: Thomas's determination. There can be no universal and particular in God, for four reasons. (1) According to Avicenna, wherever there is genus and species, quiddity must differ from being (Dist. 8), which does not fit God. (2) A universal essence is not numerically the same in its inferiors, only conceptually, whereas the divine essence is numerically the same in several persons. (3) A universal requires plurality under it, actual as in a genus, which always has several species, or potential as in some species, whose form of itself can be found in many, every form being communicable of itself, though it may be found in only one because of the matter due to that species, all united in one individual, as the sun consists of all its matter. This plurality is numerical, founded on substantial distinction, and the three persons are not numbered by such number. (4) A particular always adds to its universal, and in God, because of supreme simplicity, no addition is possible.
claims: There is no universal or particular in God: quiddity is not distinct from being, the essence is numerically one in the persons, the persons are not numbered by substantial distinction, and nothing is added to the essence.

ta-l1d19q4-d1e3619.summary: Reply to the first argument. The mode of predicating is proportioned to the things predicated, since speech is subject to the thing (Hilary). As nothing in creatures wholly resembles the unity of essence in three persons, but only in some respect, so no mode of predicating in creatures resembles the way the essence or God is predicated of the three persons. In the respect noted in the objection it resembles the predication of a universal whole, but differs in the other respects given in the body.
claims: The predication of the essence of the persons resembles universal predication only partially.

ta-l1d19q4-d1e3622.summary: Reply to the second argument. 'Common' of itself does not determine whether the community is real or conceptual, as 'universal' does, so the essence can be called common but not universal.
claims: The essence is common but not universal.

ta-l1d19q4-d1e3626.summary: Reply to the third argument. Hilary speaks after the likeness of creatures, as we commonly call the human race one 'genus' in the sense of a multitude related to one principle. Likewise the plurality of persons in their order of emanation from one principle, the Father, is called the divine 'genus'.
claims: Hilary's 'genus' means a multitude ordered to one principle, not a logical genus.

ta-l1d19q4-d1e3629.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. Some things in creatures imply perfection both by the concept of genus and of species, so both are attributed to God by their proper concepts, as cognition and science. Though they relate as genus and species in creatures, they do not in God, since one adds nothing to the other really, only conceptually.
claims: Cognition and science are said of God without relating as genus and species.

ta-l1d19q4-Dd1e3493.summary: The Prooemium of Question 4 maps Lombard's proof of the persons' equal magnitude by removing integral, universal, material, and formal-property models of their sharing the essence. It notes his reconciliation of Damascene and his proof from truth that God is triune, not triple, and announces two articles on integral and universal wholes in God.
claims: The persons share the essence in no creaturely manner of whole and parts.

ta-l1d19q4-Dd1e3545.summary: Article 1 asks whether there is an integral whole in God. Thomas holds that there is not, since integral wholes imply composition and integral parts imply imperfection. Quantity of power is divided only externally. The divine ternary signifies distinction by relations without aggregation of essences, so it is an integral whole only conceptually. The Father is 'someone' but not 'something' of the Trinity, and nothing is added to the nature to constitute a person.
claims: There is no integral whole in God; the number of persons is distinction without aggregation.

ta-l1d19q4-Dd1e3586.summary: Article 2 asks whether there is a universal whole in God. Thomas holds that there is not, for four reasons: quiddity is not distinct from being in God, the essence is numerically one in the persons, the persons are not numbered by substantial distinction, and nothing can be added to the essence. The essence is common but not universal. The predication of the essence of the persons resembles universal predication only in part, Hilary's 'genus' means a lineage from one principle, and cognition and science do not relate as genus and species in God.
claims: There is no universal or particular in God; the essence is common but not universal.

ta-l1d19q4.summary: Quaestio 4 of Book I, Distinction 19 examines Lombard's proof that the persons are equal in magnitude because they do not share the essence in any creaturely way. Article 1 holds that there is no integral whole in God, since that implies composition. The number of persons signifies distinction by opposed relations without aggregation of essences, so the Father is 'someone', not 'something', of the Trinity. Article 2 holds that there is no universal and particular in God, because quiddity is not distinct from being, the essence is numerically one in the persons, there is no substantial numbering, and nothing can be added. The divine essence is common but not universal, and its predication of the persons has no exact creaturely parallel.
claims: The divine persons share the essence neither as parts of an integral whole nor as instances of a universal.
The number of persons is distinction without aggregation.
The divine essence is common but not universal.
